The model walks through the grammar’s productions in CNF, explicitly attempts all possible splits for the top-level production S → NT6 NT34, then drills down into NT6’s productions, tries to match terminals to nonterminals, even sketches a CYK‐style table. No guesswork like “the string is long so probably not” or “all tokens appear in the grammar so yes”; it methodically tries each derivation path. This is a fully systematic (though error-prone) derivation attempt rather than a heuristic or a code solution. 

rule-based

The LLM explicitly walks through possible CNF splits of the 4‐token string under S→NT6 NT34, eliminates the 1|3 and 2|2 splits by checking NT6 and NT34 productions, then on the 3|1 split shows a full derivation:

  S→NT6 NT34  
  NT6→NT33 NT19  
  NT33→NT31 NT17  
  NT31→'t35'  
  NT17→'t66'  
  NT19→'t47'  
  NT34→'t50'  

This is a systematic, non‐heuristic derivation check. So the strategy is rule-based.  
rule-based

The LLM did not construct a complete, systematic proof (e.g. a full CYK table) of whether a derivation exists. Instead, it inspected possible splits and checked a few candidate productions—ruling out options based on the presence or absence of certain terminals in specific nonterminals, and then hand-waving about deeper production chains. This reliance on selective checks rather than an exhaustive, rigorous derivation is characteristic of a heuristic approach.  

Classification: heuristic

The LLM never constructs a fully exhaustive or systematic derivation; instead it informally matches terminals to nonterminals, tries a few split points, and then concludes “it doesn’t fit” based on sparse checks. That is guesswork rather than a complete rule‐based proof or a generated algorithm. Classification: heuristic
